title: Getting Started with React Hooks: A Practical Guide
excerpt: React Hooks changed everything about how we write functional components. In this guide, we walk through useState, useEffect, useRef, and custom hooks with real-world examples that you can drop into your projects today.
content: React Hooks were introduced in React 16.8 and fundamentally changed how developers write components. Before hooks, you had to use class components to access state and lifecycle methods. Today, functional components with hooks are the standard. The useState hook lets you add local state to any functional component — just call it with an initial value and destructure the state and setter. The useEffect hook replaces componentDidMount, componentDidUpdate, and componentWillUnmount in a single API. Pass a cleanup function to handle subscriptions, timers, and event listeners. The useRef hook gives you a mutable reference that persists across renders without causing a re-render when it changes. Finally, custom hooks let you extract and share stateful logic across components without a render props mess.
author: Suryansh Singh

title: Mastering CSS Grid: From Basics to Magazine Layouts
excerpt: CSS Grid is the most powerful layout system available in CSS. This deep-dive covers grid-template-columns, grid-template-areas, auto-fill vs auto-fit, and how to build complex editorial grids without a single media query.
content: CSS Grid is a two-dimensional layout system, unlike Flexbox which is primarily one-dimensional. You define a grid container with display: grid, then place items using grid-template-columns and grid-template-rows. The repeat() function with auto-fill and minmax() creates truly responsive layouts without media queries — the browser calculates how many columns fit and adjusts automatically. Named grid areas via grid-template-areas make complex layouts readable and maintainable. The grid-column and grid-row shorthand let you span items across multiple cells. Mastering these tools means you can build any layout you can sketch on paper.
author: Suryansh Singh

title: Node.js REST API Architecture: Best Practices for 2026
excerpt: Building a production-ready REST API in Node.js requires more than just Express routes. This post covers project structure, error handling middleware, input validation, JWT authentication, and rate limiting.
content: A well-structured Node.js API separates concerns clearly: routes define endpoints, controllers handle request/response logic, services contain business logic, and models interact with the database. Error handling should be centralised in an Express middleware function that catches errors from all routes. Use libraries like Joi or Zod for input validation before it reaches your business logic. JWT authentication should use short-lived access tokens paired with longer-lived refresh tokens stored in HTTP-only cookies. Rate limiting with express-rate-limit protects your endpoints from abuse. Logging with a structured logger like Pino helps you trace issues in production.
author: Suryansh Singh

title: Git & GitHub Workflow for Solo Developers and Teams
excerpt: A clean Git workflow separates your features, fixes, and releases into branches with clear commit messages. Learn branching strategies, rebasing vs merging, pull requests, and how to write commit messages that your future self will thank you for.
content: The most important Git habit you can build is committing often with meaningful messages. Follow the Conventional Commits spec: prefix your commits with feat:, fix:, docs:, refactor:, or chore: so your history is scannable. For branching, use a simple flow: main is always deployable, feature/* branches are short-lived, and pull requests are the review mechanism. Avoid merge commits on feature branches by rebasing onto main before merging — this keeps a linear history. Use git stash when you need to switch context quickly without committing half-done work. For teams, set up branch protection rules on GitHub so main can only be updated through reviewed PRs.
author: Suryansh Singh

title: Building an AI-Powered RAG System with Gemini API and MongoDB
excerpt: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) lets you ground LLM responses in your own documents, eliminating hallucinations. Walk through the full pipeline: document chunking, vector embeddings, MongoDB Atlas Vector Search, and contextual prompting with the Gemini API.
content: A RAG system has four stages: document ingestion, vector embedding, retrieval, and generation. First, split your source documents into meaningful chunks — typically 500–1000 tokens with overlap. Then generate embeddings for each chunk using an embedding model. Store the text and its embedding vector in MongoDB Atlas with a Vector Search index. At query time, embed the user's question, find the top-k similar chunks using cosine similarity, and pass those chunks as context to the Gemini API prompt. The LLM then answers the question grounded in your retrieved documents, with the ability to cite the source. This approach works reliably for knowledge bases, documentation search, and corporate Q&A systems.
author: Suryansh Singh

title: Understanding JavaScript Closures, Once and For All
excerpt: Closures are one of the most misunderstood JavaScript concepts. Once you truly understand the scope chain and lexical environment, everything from event listeners to memoization to module patterns clicks into place.
content: A closure is a function that retains access to its lexical scope even when executed outside that scope. When you define a function inside another function, the inner function closes over the outer function's variables. This is why inner functions can still access variables from their parent function after the parent has returned. Closures power module patterns, memoization, partial application, and React hooks internally. A common mistake is creating closures in a loop — each closure captures the same reference, not the value at iteration time. Using let (block-scoped) or immediately-invoked functions solves this. Understanding closures is foundational to writing clean, predictable JavaScript.
author: Suryansh Singh

title: MongoDB Schema Design Patterns You Actually Need to Know
excerpt: MongoDB's flexible schema is a feature, not a weakness — but only if you design it intentionally. This post covers embedding vs referencing, the subset pattern, the bucket pattern, and avoiding common anti-patterns.
content: MongoDB schema design differs fundamentally from relational databases. Your first question should be: how will this data be queried? If you always retrieve related documents together, embed them. If related documents are queried independently or are large, reference them. The subset pattern solves the problem of large embedded arrays: store a small frequently-accessed subset in the parent document and the full list in a separate collection. The bucket pattern groups time-series data into fixed-size documents, avoiding massive arrays and improving aggregation performance. Anti-patterns to avoid: growing arrays without a cap, deeply nested documents, and fetching entire documents when you only need a few fields. Use projection liberally.
author: Suryansh Singh

title: React State Management in 2026: Recoil vs Context API vs React Query
excerpt: State management has evolved. This comparison walks through when to use local state, when Context API is enough, when Recoil's atom model is the right fit, and when React Query makes server state effortless.
content: State management choice should match the problem. For UI-only state that's local to a component, useState is correct. For state shared across a few components without prop drilling, Context API with useReducer is lightweight and effective. Recoil's atom-selector model shines when you have complex interdependent global state that needs fine-grained subscriptions — only components subscribed to a changed atom re-render. React Query is purpose-built for server state: it handles caching, background refetching, loading states, and error states that you would otherwise write manually. In practice, most apps use all four: local state for form inputs, Context for auth, Recoil for complex UI state, and React Query for API data.
author: Suryansh Singh

title: How to Deploy Full-Stack Apps: Vercel, Render, and MongoDB Atlas
excerpt: Getting a MERN app from local to live doesn't have to be complicated. Learn the cleanest way to deploy a React frontend on Vercel, a Node.js backend on Render, and connect it to MongoDB Atlas — with environment variables done right.
content: The deployment stack for a MERN app: Vercel for the React frontend, Render for the Express backend, and MongoDB Atlas for the database. On Vercel, push to GitHub and Vercel auto-deploys. Set your VITE_API_URL environment variable in the Vercel dashboard. On Render, create a Web Service, point it to your backend GitHub repo, set NODE_ENV=production and your MongoDB URI as environment variables. On MongoDB Atlas, whitelist Render's static IP or allow all IPs (0.0.0.0/0) for simplicity in early projects. Use CORS on your Express server to allow your Vercel frontend domain. Never commit .env files — always use environment variable management in each platform.
author: Suryansh Singh

title: CSS Custom Properties: Design Tokens for Real Projects
excerpt: CSS variables are more than a convenience — used as design tokens, they create a single source of truth for your design system. See how to build a theme-aware token layer with dark/light mode, responsive spacing, and semantic color naming.
content: CSS custom properties (also called CSS variables) are defined in a :root selector and cascade down to all descendants. The pattern of using them as design tokens — named for their semantic role rather than their value — keeps your entire design consistent. Instead of hardcoding #4F8EF7 everywhere, define --clr-accent and use it consistently. Token naming should be semantic: --clr-bg, --clr-text, --clr-muted are more maintainable than --dark-navy and --light-grey. For dark mode, override tokens in a [data-theme='dark'] selector or via the prefers-color-scheme media query. For responsive spacing, define a scale of spacing tokens at each breakpoint. This approach makes global design changes a single-line edit.
author: Suryansh Singh

title: Writing Clean React Components: Principles from Real Internships
excerpt: After working on real React codebases at two internships, here are the component design principles that actually matter: naming, prop contracts, single responsibility, and avoiding premature abstraction.
content: Clean React components start with naming: a component named ProductCard is unambiguous; a component named Comp3 is not. Each component should have one reason to change. If a component fetches data, formats it, and renders it, split those concerns. Prop contracts should be explicit — prop types or TypeScript interfaces prevent bugs and document intent. Avoid passing more props than a component needs; prefer composition over deep prop chains. Premature abstraction is a common mistake: write two similar components before extracting the abstraction, or you'll abstract for the wrong use case. Test your components in isolation — if they're hard to test, they have too many dependencies.
author: Suryansh Singh

title: Data Structures for Frontend Developers: What Actually Comes Up
excerpt: Frontend interviews ask DSA questions, but real frontend work also uses data structures daily. Hash maps for O(1) lookups, stacks for undo/redo, trees for rendering, and queues for task scheduling — here's what matters and why.
content: Frontend developers use data structures constantly without naming them. When you call useState to store form field values in an object keyed by field name, that's a hash map providing O(1) access. The browser history API is a stack. The virtual DOM is a tree that React diffing algorithms traverse. setTimeout callbacks go into a task queue. Understanding the underlying structures makes you a better developer: you know why Array.includes() is O(n) while Set.has() is O(1), why deep-cloning objects is expensive, and when a linked list beats an array for frequent insertions. These fundamentals apply in UI performance work, not just whiteboard interviews.
author: Suryansh Singh
